content.text: Frontend HTTP routes are a clean place to look for a path-specific change, so I'll compare duration and status codes per route in each period.

input.query: SELECT 'norm' p, span_name, attr_http_response_status_code st, count(*) n, round(quantile_cont(duration,0.5)/1e6,3) p50, round(quantile_cont(duration,0.95)/1e6,3) p95 FROM normal_traces WHERE service_name='frontend' AND attr_span_kind='Server' GROUP BY 1,2,3 UNION ALL SELECT 'abn', span_name, attr_http_response_status_code, count(*), round(quantile_cont(duration,0.5)/1e6,3), round(quantile_cont(duration,0.95)/1e6,3) FROM abnormal_traces WHERE service_name='frontend' AND attr_span_kind='Server' GROUP BY 1,2,3 ORDER BY 2,1

content.text: The `/hotels` route's p50 fell from 7.1 ms to 2.7 ms while p95 held, so part of that route is getting fast. I'll test whether search's Server spans link to frontend's search client spans within the same trace.

input.query: SELECT 'norm' p, count(*) search_servers, sum(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM normal_traces f WHERE f.trace_id=s.trace_id AND f.span_id=s.parent_span_id) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) parent_in_same_trace, sum(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM normal_traces f WHERE f.span_id=s.parent_span_id) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) parent_anywhere, sum(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM normal_traces f WHERE f.trace_id=s.trace_id) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) trace_present FROM normal_traces s WHERE service_name='search' AND attr_span_kind='Server' UNION ALL SELECT 'abn', count(*), sum(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM abnormal_traces f WHERE f.trace_id=s.trace_id AND f.span_id=s.parent_span_id) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), sum(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM abnormal_traces f WHERE f.span_id=s.parent_span_id) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), sum(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM abnormal_traces f WHERE f.trace_id=s.trace_id) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM abnormal_traces s WHERE service_name='search' AND attr_span_kind='Server'

content.text: Only 18 of 340 abnormal search Server spans link to a parent in their trace, versus 811 of 972 normally. I'll check whether the orphaned callees share a trace ID with a frontend client span, which would suggest a broken span-ID link rather than missing traces.

input.query: SELECT 'norm' p, s.service_name, s.span_name, count(*) n, sum(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM normal_traces c WHERE c.trace_id=s.trace_id AND c.attr_span_kind='Client' AND c.span_name=s.span_name) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) same_trace_client_exists, sum(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM normal_traces c WHERE c.trace_id=s.trace_id AND c.span_id=s.parent_span_id) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) parent_linked FROM normal_traces s WHERE s.attr_span_kind='Server' AND s.service_name IN ('profile','rate','reservation') GROUP BY 1,2,3 UNION ALL SELECT 'abn', s.service_name, s.span_name, count(*), sum(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM abnormal_traces c WHERE c.trace_id=s.trace_id AND c.attr_span_kind='Client' AND c.span_name=s.span_name) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), sum(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM abnormal_traces c WHERE c.trace_id=s.trace_id AND c.span_id=s.parent_span_id) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM abnormal_traces s WHERE s.attr_span_kind='Server' AND s.service_name IN ('profile','rate','reservation') GROUP BY 1,2,3

content.text: In the abnormal window only about 10% of callee Server spans link to a client span, versus about 80% normally, so the trace linkage itself is degraded. To see whether this follows the search CPU surge, I'll build a per-minute timeline for search CPU, search latency and frontend `/hotels` latency.

input.query: WITH cpu AS (SELECT date_trunc('minute', time) m, avg(value) cpu FROM abnormal_metrics WHERE metric='container.cpu.usage' AND service_name='search' GROUP BY 1), tr AS (SELECT date_trunc('minute', time) m, sum(CASE WHEN service_name='search' AND attr_span_kind='Server' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) search_srv, round(quantile_cont(CASE WHEN service_name='search' AND attr_span_kind='Server' THEN duration END,0.5)/1e6,2) search_p50, round(quantile_cont(CASE WHEN service_name='frontend' AND span_name='HTTP /hotels' THEN duration END,0.5)/1e6,2) hotels_p50, round(quantile_cont(CASE WHEN service_name='frontend' AND span_name='HTTP /hotels' THEN duration END,0.95)/1e6,2) hotels_p95, sum(CASE WHEN span_name='HTTP /hotels' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) hotels_n, sum(CASE WHEN span_name='HTTP /restaurants' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) rest_n FROM abnormal_traces GROUP BY 1) SELECT cpu.m, round(cpu,3) cpu, search_srv, search_p50, hotels_n, hotels_p50, hotels_p95, rest_n FROM cpu FULL JOIN tr USING (m) ORDER BY 1

content.text: Search CPU is pinned from the first minute, yet search and `/hotels` latency stay flat or fall, so CPU alone doesn't explain user impact. Next I'll compare internal and database-facing span durations for the backend services, which may show where time shifted.

input.query: SELECT 'norm' p, service_name, span_name, count(*) n, round(quantile_cont(duration,0.5)/1e6,3) p50, round(quantile_cont(duration,0.95)/1e6,3) p95, round(avg(duration)/1e6,3) avg_ms FROM normal_traces WHERE attr_span_kind='Internal' GROUP BY 1,2,3 UNION ALL SELECT 'abn', service_name, span_name, count(*), round(quantile_cont(duration,0.5)/1e6,3), round(quantile_cont(duration,0.95)/1e6,3), round(avg(duration)/1e6,3) FROM abnormal_traces WHERE attr_span_kind='Internal' GROUP BY 1,2,3 ORDER BY 2,3,1

content.text: Memcached-facing spans show a fast mode (p50 near 0.003 ms) that normal traces don't have, and traces are fragmenting: about 8 spans per trace normally versus about 4.4 abnormally. I'll check which services' spans end up in traces that lack a frontend root.

input.query: WITH t AS (SELECT 'norm' p, * FROM normal_traces UNION ALL SELECT 'abn', * FROM abnormal_traces), tr AS (SELECT p, trace_id, bool_or(service_name='frontend' AND attr_span_kind='Server') has_front, count(*) spans FROM t GROUP BY 1,2) SELECT t.p, t.service_name, t.attr_span_kind, count(*) n, sum(CASE WHEN tr.has_front THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) in_frontend_trace, round(avg(tr.spans),2) avg_spans_in_trace FROM t JOIN tr ON t.p=tr.p AND t.trace_id=tr.trace_id WHERE t.attr_span_kind IN ('Server','Client') GROUP BY 1,2,3 ORDER BY 2,3,1

content.text: Nearly all downstream spans (search, profile, rate, reservation, recommendation, user) now sit in traces without a frontend root, which points to a systematic propagation break rather than per-service faults. **Verdict: the evidence does not support `container_cpu_saturated` as stated. The closest kind is `process_cpu_saturated`, at low-to-moderate confidence.** The telemetry cannot confirm the container limit, which the claim depends on.

**What supports a CPU ceiling**
- Search container CPU (`container.cpu.usage`) goes from about 0.006 cores to a flat plateau of 2.84–2.86 cores within about 20 seconds of the abnormal window opening, and stays there for the whole window. A plateau that sits just under 3 cores is what a cgroup limit would look like.
- Pod and container CPU are identical, and there is no sign of node-level CPU pressure (`k8s.pod.cpu.node.utilization` ≈ 0.09).

**What argues against `container_cpu_saturated`**
- **No cgroup limit metric exists in this case.** Nothing shows the ceiling or the headroom, so "pinned at the limit" is inferred from the flat plateau alone.
- **Search's own work did not slow.** `container_cpu_saturated` should slow every thread inside the container. Search's Server span for `search.Search/Nearby` went from p50 4.22 ms to 3.18 ms, and its own p95 went from 6.0 to 6.7 ms. Those are not the signs of a service whose threads are all starved.
- **The CPU burn is not tied to request load.** Calls into search fell by roughly 70% across the board (frontend→search 263.6 → 81.4 calls/min, search→geo and search→rate down the same way), and the frontend itself is unaffected. Search's CPU went up about 450× while its work fell. That points to a background burn inside the search process, not a load-driven saturation of the whole container.
- **Downstream calls are normal.** Search→geo is unchanged (p50 0.4 ms), and search→rate's Client p50 went down (3.7 → 2.7 ms), so nothing on search's outgoing side shows a fault.

**Reading**
The best fit is `process_cpu_saturated`: one process inside the search container is burning about 2.85 cores without slowing the requests it serves. Search's container is effectively one process, so the two kinds cannot be fully separated here. The main thing that would decide it is the container's CPU limit and whether the container has headroom. This case does not record that, so I would not present `container_cpu_saturated` as established. Confidence is low to moderate.

**Not checked:** the search log bodies. The `abnormal_logs` table has 1,448 rows for search, but the template column came back empty, so I could not read the messages. Reading them might show what the process is doing.
